Calculus

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Analysis Real analysis
OurBigBook.com Words: 24k Articles: 341
Calculus connects local change with accumulated change. A derivative asks how fast a function changes near one input; an integral adds its contributions across an interval. The fundamental theorem of calculus explains why these operations fit together: accumulating a continuous rate produces a quantity whose derivative is that rate.
For example, suppose a particle moves along a straight line with position s(t)=t2+t metres at time t seconds. Its velocity is s′(t)=2t+1 metres per second. Between t=0 and t=3, adding the velocity over time gives
∫03​(2t+1)dt=s(3)−s(0)=12 metres.
(1)
Here the velocity stays positive, so the displacement also equals the distance travelled. If the particle reverses direction, the integral of its signed velocity still gives displacement, while the integral of its speed gives total distance.
This is useful because local rules are often easier to specify than whole trajectories. A differential equation can prescribe a particle's velocity or a population's growth rate; integration then reconstructs its evolution, subject to an initial condition. In the other direction, a derivative extracts local information from a known function, and optimization uses that information to locate or approach promising inputs. The same two operations therefore connect measurement, prediction and design.
The visual connection is developed in derivative, integral and fundamental theorem of calculus. The definitions depend on limits, which turn progressively finer finite measurements into exact mathematical statements. A graph with a corner need not have a derivative there, and the conditions permitting integration or interchange of limits matter; calculus is more than a collection of symbolic rules.
Historically, Isaac Newton described changing quantities and their rates in the language of fluents and fluxions; his manuscript History of the Method of Fluxions records that approach.[ref] Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz's Nova methodus pro maximis et minimis appeared in Acta Eruditorum in October 1684, pp. 467–473; the original article is preserved in the HKUST Library collection.[ref] The modern limit definitions used here should not be read back into those seventeenth-century formulations.

Differential calculus

Words: 34
Calculus OurBigBook.com
Differential calculus studies derivatives: how a function changes near an input and how that local information describes its graph or evolution. Its tools include linear approximation, higher derivatives, and Taylor series; applications include finding velocity from position and studying optimization through critical points.

Floor and ceiling functions (⌊x⌋,⌈x⌉)

Words: 2k Articles: 6
Calculus OurBigBook.com
The floor function and ceiling function turn a real number into directed integer bounds. They answer two different questions: which integer is the largest one that does not exceed x, and which is the smallest one that is not less than x?
⌊x⌋≤x<⌊x⌋+1,⌈x⌉−1<x≤⌈x⌉.
(2)
Both outputs are integers. These are exact mathematical operations; they need not choose the closest integer, and they do not refer to roundoff error in floating-point arithmetic.
For example,
x2.72−2.7−2​⌊x⌋22−3−2​⌈x⌉32−2−2​{x}0.700.30​​
(3)
The fractional part is {x}=x−⌊x⌋. The negative example matters: discarding the digits after the decimal point would give −2, which is truncation toward zero, rather than the floor function's value −3. At an integer, the floor function and ceiling function agree and the fractional part vanishes.
The usefulness is a bridge from continuous quantities to discrete decisions. An integer count in a closed interval uses both bounds. A ceiling count for fixed-size batches counts how many containers or pages are needed; a floor function counts how many complete groups fit. In Euclidean division, the same bounds specify the quotient, while the fractional part records the scaled remainder. A small amount of notation removes many cases that would otherwise have to be stated separately.
The reflection identity
⌈x⌉=−⌊−x⌋
(4)
follows by reflecting the ordered integers across zero: the largest one below −x becomes the smallest one above x. For every integer m, translation gives ⌊x+m⌋=⌊x⌋+m and ⌈x+m⌉=⌈x⌉+m. These formulas turn upper bounds into lower bounds and move examples between neighboring intervals.
For a historical example of the notation in use, Kenneth E. Iverson's 1962 conference paper A Programming Language lists the floor function, ceiling function and residue operation alongside the ordinary arithmetic operations. It states the two defining inequalities above, then extends operations component by component to vectors and matrices. This shows their role as tools for describing algorithms, rather than merely conventions for writing decimal numbers. [ref]

Integer count in a closed interval (∣[a,b]∩Z∣=max(0,⌊b⌋−⌈a⌉+1))

Words: 140
Floor and ceiling functions OurBigBook.com
For real numbers a≤b, the integers in the closed interval [a,b] begin at ⌈a⌉ and end at ⌊b⌋, if there are any. Their number is therefore
∣[a,b]∩Z∣=max(0,⌊b⌋−⌈a⌉+1).
(5)
The extra one includes both ends of the resulting integer interval. The maximum with zero handles an empty intersection: [0.2,0.8] contains no integer, even though it has positive length.
For [−2.7,1.1], the ceiling function selects −2 and the floor function selects 1, giving 1−(−2)+1=4. The four points are −2,−1,0,1. For [−2,2], the count is five, not four: the real length 2−(−2) and the number of integer points are different quantities.
The endpoint convention matters. For the half-open interval [a,b) with a≤b, the last allowed integer is ⌈b⌉−1, so the count becomes max(0,⌈b⌉−⌈a⌉). This handles an integer endpoint b without including it accidentally. For example, [−2,2) has four integer points.

Floor function (⌊x⌋)

Words: 218 Articles: 1
Floor and ceiling functions OurBigBook.com
The floor ⌊x⌋ is the greatest integer not exceeding the real number x. Equivalently, ⌊x⌋=m exactly when m≤x<m+1, for an integer m. The floor function is constant on each such half-open interval and has a discontinuity of a function at each integer.
For nonnegative integers N and positive integers k, ⌊N/k⌋ is the number of complete groups of size k that fit into N items. With N=102 and k=20, five complete groups use 100 items. Euclidean division writes 102=20⋅5+2, retaining the two-item remainder rather than treating the quotient 102/20=5.1 as a number of complete groups.

Fractional part ({x})

Words: 130
Floor function OurBigBook.com
The fractional part of a real number is
{x}=x−⌊x⌋∈[0,1).
(6)
It is the amount left after removing the lower enclosing integer, even for negative inputs. Thus {−2.7}=−2.7−(−3)=0.3. It is not the signed string of digits obtained by truncation toward zero.
Translation by an integer leaves the fractional part unchanged: {x+m}={x}. It is therefore a periodic function with period one, increasing from zero toward one on each unit interval, then returning to zero at the next integer. In Euclidean division N=kq+r with 0≤r<k, {N/k}=r/k; for 102/20, this is 2/20=0.1.
The notation is useful for following repeated motion modulo an integer. In normality and equidistribution under integer multiplication, the values {Knx} shift the digits of a positional notation; the fractional part discards the leading integer portion without losing the remaining digits. Its braces must be distinguished by context from the braces denoting a set.

Ceiling function (⌈x⌉)

Words: 524 Articles: 1
Floor and ceiling functions OurBigBook.com
The ceiling function gives the least integer large enough to meet a real lower bound. For a real number x,
⌈x⌉=m⟺m−1<x≤m,m∈Z.
(7)
Thus ⌈2.7⌉=3, ⌈−2.7⌉=−2, and ⌈2⌉=2. The operation rounds upward in the total order on the real numbers, which can move a negative input towards zero. Its difference from the input obeys 0≤⌈x⌉−x<1. Python's math.ceil implements this least-integer definition. [ref].
The ceiling count for fixed-size batches is a direct application. Suppose each box holds at most k items, with positive integer k, and there are N≥0 items. The smallest number of boxes with enough capacity is ⌈N/k⌉: a candidate count b must satisfy bk≥N. For N=101, k=20, six boxes are needed, leaving 120−101=19 unused places. Exactly 100 items need only five boxes, and zero items need zero boxes. Adding one to the floor function result unconditionally would therefore overcount at exact multiples of k.
For nonnegative integer N and positive integer k, Euclidean division gives the exact identity
⌈kN​⌉=⌊kN+k−1​⌋.​
(8)
Write N=qk+r, 0≤r<k. The count is q when the remainder is zero and q+1 otherwise, and the right-hand side encodes these two cases. This argument specifies the domain of the identity; arbitrary negative denominators require their own sign conventions.
The ceiling function is a nondecreasing function, constant on each of the half-open intervals (m−1,m], and has a discontinuity of a function at every integer. It is tied to the floor function by ⌈x⌉=−⌊−x⌋. Adding an integer j shifts its output by the same amount: ⌈x+j⌉=⌈x⌉+j. At an integer the floor and ceiling agree; at every other input they differ by one. These statements refer to exact real numbers; an input already perturbed by floating-point arithmetic can land on the other side of a threshold.

Ceiling count for fixed-size batches (b=⌈N/k⌉)

Words: 174
Ceiling function OurBigBook.com
Suppose N is a nonnegative integer count of items and each batch holds at most k items, where k is a positive integer. The smallest sufficient number of batches is
b=⌈kN​⌉.
(9)
Indeed, bk≥N exactly when the integer b is at least N/k. If N=0, no batches are needed. If N is a multiple of k, no partly filled batch is needed.
For 102 items with capacity 20 per batch, b=⌈5.1⌉=6. Five batches can be full and the sixth holds two items, leaving 6⋅20−102=18 unused places. This is a different question from the five complete groups counted by ⌊102/20⌋.
Writing the Euclidean division N=kq+r, 0≤r<k, gives the equivalent rule b=q when r=0, and b=q+1 when r>0. This explains the ceiling function's jump: one extra item beyond a complete multiple demands a whole additional batch. For exact integer arithmetic, the identity b=⌊(N+k−1)/k⌋ avoids a fractional intermediate value; an implementation still needs an integer representation large enough to hold N+k−1.

Truncation toward zero (trunc(x)={⌊x⌋⌈x⌉​x≥0x<0​)

Words: 293
Floor and ceiling functions OurBigBook.com
Truncation toward zero removes the fractional magnitude of a real number, giving the integer obtained by applying the floor function to its absolute value and restoring the original sign; a magnitude below one gives zero. More precisely,
trunc(x)={⌊x⌋⌈x⌉​x≥0,x<0.​
(10)
The result is zero for −1<x<1. For example, trunc(2.7)=2 and trunc(−2.7)=−2, whereas ⌊−2.7⌋=−3. Python's math.trunc uses this towards-zero convention, so replacing it by math.floor changes calculations with negative noninteger inputs. [ref].
For every real number x,
∣x−trunc(x)∣<1,trunc(−x)=−trunc(x).
(11)
The discarded difference x−trunc(x) has the sign of x when x is noninteger. In contrast, the fractional part x−⌊x⌋ is always in [0,1). At x=−2.7, these two differences are −0.7 and 0.3. Thus specifying a signed fractional remainder requires specifying which integer-valued operation is used.
Unlike the floor function and ceiling function, truncation toward zero need not commute with adding an integer. At x=−0.7 and j=1, trunc(x+j)=trunc(0.3)=0, whereas trunc(x)+j=1. This matters if negative coordinates are assigned to equal-width bins by converting a quotient to an integer: x=−0.7 belongs to the bin [−1,0) under the floor function, but truncation gives zero. The appropriate operation follows from the declared bin intervals.
Truncation toward zero is a nondecreasing function with a discontinuity of a function at each nonzero integer. It has no discontinuity of a function at zero, because it is identically zero on (−1,1). Its agreement with the floor function on the positive side and the ceiling function on the negative side explains the different closed endpoints in the diagram.

Integral (∫)

Words: 3k Articles: 35
Calculus OurBigBook.com
An integral adds up contributions of a function across a domain. For a continuous function f on [a,b], the Riemann integral is the common limit of its Riemann sums as the largest subinterval width tends to zero:
∫ab​f(x)dx=limmaxi​Δxi​→0​∑i​f(ξi​)Δxi​,ξi​∈[xi−1​,xi​],Δxi​=xi​−xi−1​.
(12)
Each product combines a value with the width over which it acts. When f is nonnegative, the result is the area beneath its graph; values below the horizontal axis contribute with the opposite sign. The signed area under a graph can therefore vanish even when the graph encloses nonzero geometric area.
For a velocity v(t)=1+2t on 0≤t≤3, use n equal time steps. The left and right Riemann sums are
Ln​=12−n9​,Rn​=12+n9​.
(13)
Because the function is increasing, they bound the integral. With six steps they give 10.5 and 13.5; with sixty steps they give 11.85 and 12.15. Both approach the same total, 12. This is accumulation made exact by refining finite measurements.
An integral retains units: velocity times time gives displacement, and a probability density function integrated over an interval gives a probability. Weighting a density by a function gives its expectation. The same operation serves different subjects because it expresses a common pattern, value multiplied by extent, then accumulated.
The fundamental theorem of calculus often evaluates a definite integral by finding an antiderivative, but a finite sum or a numerical approximation is still useful when no convenient antiderivative is available. An indefinite integral denotes a family of antiderivatives; a definite integral denotes an accumulated value between specified endpoints. More general constructions, including Lebesgue integration, extend the class of functions and domains that can be handled.

Average value of a function (f​I​=∣I∣−1∫I​f(x)dx)

Words: 118
Integral OurBigBook.com
For an integrable function on an interval I of positive finite length, its average value is the integral divided by that length:
f​I​=∣I∣1​∫I​f(x)dx.
(14)
If f is constant on equal-length subintervals, this is their values' arithmetic mean; unequal lengths require a weighted mean. For example, values 2 and 6 on two equal halves give average value 4, whereas value 2 on the first quarter and 6 on the remaining three quarters give 5. The integral measures total contribution; the average value of a function divides out the interval length.
For the function f(x)=2x on [0,1], the average value of a function is ∫01​2xdx=1. Replacing it by the constant 1 preserves its integral on this interval. This is why the Haar projection uses cell averages to obtain a coarser description while retaining each cell's total contribution.

Linearity of integration (∫(af+bg)dμ=a∫fdμ+b∫gdμ)

Words: 118
Integral OurBigBook.com
For integrable real-valued functions f,g on a measure space (X,μ) and fixed real numbers a,b, their linear combination af+bg is integrable, and the Lebesgue integral satisfies
∫X​(af+bg)dμ=a∫X​fdμ+b∫X​gdμ.
(15)
The same rule applies to any finite summation: ∫X​∑j=1n​aj​fj​dμ=∑j=1n​aj​∫X​fj​dμ for integrable functions fj​ and fixed scalars aj​. Finite signed values matter: integrability ensures all these integrals are finite, so no undefined ∞−∞ occurs.
This is the distributive property of finite summation carried into integration: a fixed factor can be pulled out, and a finite sum can be integrated term by term. For simple functions, distribute the finite sums of value times measure; approximation extends additivity to nonnegative measurable functions, and splitting into a positive part and negative part gives the integrable signed case. See Lecture 12: Lebesgue Integrable Functions, the Lebesgue Integral and the Dominated Convergence Theorem (Proposition 122: linearity for integrable functions). For example, ∫01​(2x−3)dx=2∫01​xdx−3∫01​1dx=−2. With a probability measure, linearity of integration gives linearity of expectation.

Signed area under a graph (∫ab​f(x)dx)

Words: 251 Articles: 1
Integral OurBigBook.com
For a<b and a real-valued function f with a finite Riemann integral or Lebesgue integral on [a,b], the signed area under a graph is its definite integral: geometric area above the horizontal axis contributes positively, and geometric area below it contributes negatively. If these two nonnegative areas are A+​ and A−​, then
∫ab​f(x)dx=A+​−A−​,∫ab​∣f(x)∣dx=A+​+A−​.
(16)
The second expression is the total geometric area under a graph. Taking the absolute value of the first expression does not usually give the second: cancellation has already removed information about how much area lies on each side.[ref]
For an exact example, take the polynomial function f(x)=x2−1 on [−2,2]. Its polynomial roots are −1 and 1: it is negative between them and positive on the two outer intervals. An antiderivative is F(x)=x3/3−x, so the fundamental theorem of calculus gives
∫−2−1​(x2−1)dx=34​,∫−11​(x2−1)dx=−34​,∫12​(x2−1)dx=34​.
(17)
Thus A+​=8/3 and A−​=4/3. The signed area under a graph is 4/3, whereas the total geometric area under a graph is 4. To compute the latter with antiderivatives, split at each sign-changing polynomial root and reverse the sign of the negative contribution.
Cancellation is useful information when the integrand represents a signed contribution. For the polynomial function f(x)=x on [−1,1], the two triangular areas give ∫−11​xdx=0, although ∫−11​∣x∣dx=1. Zero net signed area therefore means balanced positive and negative contributions, rather than an empty region.
The short algebraic justification uses the positive part f+​=max(f,0) and negative part f−​=max(−f,0): f=f+​−f−​ and ∣f∣=f+​+f−​. Their integrals give A+​ and A−​, and linearity of integration gives the difference and sum formulas. For Lebesgue integration, require both contributions to be finite to avoid the undefined subtraction ∞−∞.[ref]

Definite integral (∫ab​f(x)dx)

Words: 517 Articles: 1
Integral OurBigBook.com
A definite integral accumulates an integrand between specified endpoints, retaining the sign of each contribution. For a real-valued function on a finite real interval, a finite definite integral is a scalar; an indefinite integral describes a family of antiderivatives. The lower and upper limits of integration a,b specify where accumulation starts and ends. The integration variable is a placeholder: ∫ab​f(x)dx=∫ab​f(u)du.
This is useful whenever a varying rate must be converted into a total change. For motion along a straight line with continuous velocity v(t) and position s(t) satisfying s′(t)=v(t), the fundamental theorem of calculus gives displacement, while accumulating speed gives the distance traveled from velocity:
s(b)−s(a)=∫ab​v(t)dt,D=∫ab​∣v(t)∣dt,a<b.
(18)
Negative velocity reduces displacement while adding to the distance traveled from velocity. The physical dimension of a definite integral is the product of the integrand's physical dimension and the integration variable's physical dimension: here (m/s)s=m. An area on a rate graph need not be a spatial area.[ref]
As an explicitly synthetic motion model, let v(t)=(2ms−2)t−2ms−1 for 0≤t≤3s, with s(0)=0. Using numerical values in seconds and metres, an antiderivative gives s(t)=t2−2t. The velocity changes sign at t=1: the model first moves 1 m in the negative direction, then 4 m in the positive direction. Its displacement is −1+4=3 m, and its distance traveled from velocity is 1+4=5 m. The initial position fixes the constant of integration, but does not change either accumulated quantity.
Orientation matters independently of whether the integrand is positive or negative. For a function integrable on the interval containing the endpoints, use the conventions
∫aa​f(x)dx=0,∫ba​f(x)dx=−∫ab​f(x)dx,∫ac​f(x)dx=∫ab​f(x)dx+∫bc​f(x)dx.
(19)
For the preceding velocity model, accumulation from 3 seconds back to 0 seconds gives −3 m. Reversing the bounds of the speed integral gives −5 m, which is an oriented integral, not a negative distance traveled from velocity; physical elapsed-time totals use the earlier endpoint first. The splitting rule holds even when b is outside the interval between a and c, provided integrability holds on the interval containing all three endpoints.[ref]
Existence needs hypotheses. For a bounded function f on [a,b] with a<b, a finite Riemann integral exists when every tagged Riemann sum approaches the same value as the largest cell width tends to zero:
∫ab​f(x)dx=limmaxi​(xi​−xi−1​)→0​∑i=1n​f(ξi​)(xi​−xi−1​),a=x0​<⋯<xn​=b,ξi​∈[xi−1​,xi​].
(20)
The limit must be independent of both the partition of an interval and the tags. Merely making the number of cells large can leave a wide cell unresolved. On a finite closed interval, every continuous function, and every bounded function that is continuous except at finitely many points, is Riemann integrable.[ref] Boundedness alone is insufficient: the Dirichlet function on [0,1] is 1 on the rational numbers and 0 on the irrational numbers. Tags can all be chosen rational or all irrational, giving Riemann sums of 1 or 0 at arbitrarily small cell widths.[ref]
For a finite signed Lebesgue integral, the condition is instead that f be a measurable function for Lebesgue measure and ∫[a,b]​∣f∣dx<∞. A measurable function for Lebesgue measure that is also a bounded function on a finite interval satisfies this condition since ∣f∣≤M gives ∫∣f∣≤M(b−a). The Dirichlet function therefore has Lebesgue integral zero: the rational numbers form a null set, so it equals zero Lebesgue almost everywhere. The Riemann integral and Lebesgue integral agree for the continuous functions used in the diagrams.[ref] An unbounded integrand or infinite endpoint requires further analysis, for example the limits defining an improper integral; the notation alone does not establish convergence.

I2n​=22n(n!)2(2n)!​2π​,I2n+1​=(2n+1)!22n(n!)2​.

Integral OurBigBook.com
A multiple integral accumulates a function over a region with several coordinates. The Fubini theorem and Tonelli theorem give conditions under which it equals successive one-dimensional integrals. A change of variables formula expresses it in new coordinates using the absolute Jacobian determinant.

Odd-integrand cancellation by reflection

Words: 57
Multiple integral OurBigBook.com
If a region is invariant under one coordinate reflection and an integrable function changes sign under that reflection, its multiple integral is zero. Apply the change of variables formula to the reflection, whose absolute Jacobian determinant is one: the integral equals its negative. This applies to odd coordinate powers in symmetric volumes and to the off-diagonal entries of an inertia tensor when the mass density shares the coordinate-reflection symmetries.

Antiderivative (F′=g)

Words: 641 Articles: 3
Integral OurBigBook.com
An antiderivative recovers a function from its local rate of change. For a real-valued function g on an open subset U of the real line, a differentiable function F is an antiderivative when
F′(x)=g(x)(x∈U).​
(24)
For example, g(x)=x2 has the antiderivatives FC​(x)=x3/3+C for every real additive constant C. Their derivatives agree, while their values can differ. On an interval, the constant of integration describes the entire freedom in the answer. [ref]
The indefinite-integral notation ∫g(x)dx=F(x)+C records this family on an interval. For the illustrated family, the extra condition F(1)=2 selects C=5/3. Thus reversing differentiation requires both a rate and a reference value if a unique function is wanted.
The fundamental theorem of calculus supplies a construction when g is continuous on an interval I. Choose x0​∈I and set F(x)=∫x0​x​g(t)dt; then F′=g. Integrability alone does not guarantee a classical antiderivative. The Heaviside step function is Riemann integrable on bounded intervals, but cannot be a derivative throughout an interval containing its jump: Darboux theorem for derivatives requires every intermediate value. [ref]

Constant of integration (∫f(x)dx=F(x)+C)

Words: 341 Articles: 1
Antiderivative OurBigBook.com
On a connected open interval, if F′=g, every antiderivative of g has the form F+C, where C is a constant function. Indeed, two solutions satisfy (G−F)′=0: the zero derivative on a connected open set principle makes their difference constant. In one dimension, the mean value theorem proves this on any closed subinterval. [ref]
An initial condition or boundary condition can determine C. If a particular antiderivative is F0​ and F(x0​)=y0​, then
C=y0​−F0​(x0​).​
(25)
For g(x)=x2, F0​(x)=x3/3 and F(1)=2, this gives C=5/3. Without that reference value, choosing C=0 simply selects one member of the family.
The freedom has a physical meaning in a simple kinematic model. A velocity v(t)=at, with constant acceleration a, determines position only as x(t)=at2/2+C. The initial condition x(0)=x0​ selects C=x0​; changing the starting position does not change the prescribed velocity.
For the differential equation T′=−B/r2 on r>0, the antiderivative is T=B/r+C. The boundary condition T(Rs​)=Ts​ gives C=Ts​−B/Rs​. Discarding the constant of integration therefore needs a specified condition or an approximation that quantifies its effect. On a domain with several connected components, the freedom is larger: antiderivatives on disconnected domains require a separate constant on each component.
Antiderivatives on disconnected domains ((G−F)∣Ij​​=Cj​)
Words: 164
Constant of integration OurBigBook.com
Let U be an open subset of the real line, and let F,G be antiderivatives of the same function on U. Each connected component Ij​ is an open interval. On that component, (G−F)′=0, so the mean value theorem gives G−F=Cj​. The constants on different components are independent: there is no subinterval inside U joining them. Conversely, adding any chosen constant on each component preserves the derivative everywhere on U.
For example, the domain of g(x)=1/x is U=R∖{0}. Every antiderivative on this domain has the form
F(x)={log∣x∣+C−​,log∣x∣+C+​,​x<0,x>0,​
(26)
with arbitrary real C−​,C+​. The logarithm of the absolute value differentiates to 1/x on each side. The function with C−​=2 and C+​=−1 is therefore a valid antiderivative, although it cannot be written as log∣x∣+C with one global constant.
An initial condition at x=1 fixes C+​ and leaves C−​ free. Fixing both constants requires one reference value in each connected component, or additional conditions that couple the components. The locally constant function F(x)−log∣x∣ captures this remaining freedom.

Additive constant (F(x)+C)

Words: 126
Antiderivative OurBigBook.com
A constant added to a function changes its reference level without changing its derivative:
dxd​(F(x)+C)=F′(x).
(27)
Geometrically, it is a vertical translation of the graph. For F(x)=x3/3, changing C moves every plotted value by the same amount while preserving every tangent slope. This is the geometric reason that antiderivatives form a family.
When F represents a physical quantity, the physical dimension of C must match that of F. When position is obtained from velocity, C is a position offset. An unknown starting position remains unknown even when the rate of change is known exactly.
When describing the family of antiderivatives on an interval, the arbitrary additive constant is the constant of integration. On a disconnected open domain, the corresponding freedom is a locally constant function, as in antiderivatives on disconnected domains, rather than necessarily one constant on the whole domain.

Gaussian integral (∫−∞∞​e−x2dx=π​)

Integral OurBigBook.com
The Gaussian integral gives the exact area under a Gaussian function. For a positive real number a,
I(a)=∫−∞∞​e−ax2dx=aπ​​.​
(28)
This is a finite improper integral over the whole real line. For example, I(1)=π​≈1.772454 and I(4)=π​/2≈0.886227. Increasing a from one to four narrows the curve and halves its area, while its height at zero stays one. The change of variables u=a​x explains the factor a−1/2.
The useful consequence is an exact normalization. For a>0 and any real center μ,
pa​(x)=πa​​e−a(x−μ)2,∫R​pa​(x)dx=1.
(29)
This is a probability density function for a normal distribution with expected value μ and variance 1/(2a). A narrower probability density function must be taller to keep total probability one. In the usual notation a=1/(2σ2), the prefactor is 1/(σ2π​), where σ is the standard deviation.
The same area calculation makes the one-dimensional heat kernel
K(x,t)=4πDt​1​e−x2/(4Dt),D>0,t>0,
(30)
integrate to one in x, with D the diffusion coefficient. A spreading Gaussian function can therefore preserve total mass while its height falls. This links the Gaussian integral with both the normal distribution and the diffusion equation.
Finite intervals lead to the error function, rather than this single constant:
erf(z)=π​2​∫0z​e−u2du,∫−RR​e−ax2dx=aπ​​erf(a​R),R≥0.
(31)
The complementary tail is described by the complementary error function. These definitions and their real-axis limits are given in the NIST reference. [ref]
The polar-coordinate proof of the Gaussian integral explains why π appears in an integral of a function defined on a line: squaring its area creates a rotationally symmetric integral on a plane. Substitution t=x2 also gives Γ(1/2)=2∫0∞​e−x2dx=π​, connecting the result with the Gamma function.

A Taylor polynomial replaces a function near a chosen point by a polynomial with matching derivatives. If f has derivatives through order n at a, define
Tn,a​(x)=∑k=0n​k!f(k)(a)​(x−a)k.
(35)
The factorial denominator makes Tn,a(j)​(a)=f(j)(a) for 0≤j≤n. This determines a unique polynomial of degree of a polynomial at most n. Order zero matches the value, order one also matches the tangent line, and order two also incorporates the second derivative. Matching more local information is useful because polynomials are easy to evaluate, differentiate, and integrate. The distinction between the finite Taylor polynomial and the infinite Taylor series is developed in OpenStax, Taylor and Maclaurin series.
For a computed example, let f(x)=1+x​ and expand at zero. Its first three derivatives give
f(0)=1,f′(0)=21​,f′′(0)=−41​,T2,0​(x)=1+2x​−8x2​.

Exponential function (ex)

The real exponential function exp(x)=ex converts addition into multiplication:
exp(x+y)=exp(x)exp(y),exp(0)=1,dxd​exp(x)=exp(x).

Its values are positive, and it defines a bijection from the real numbers to the positive real numbers. The natural logarithm is its inverse function. These properties connect arithmetic with calculus: adding an amount to the input multiplies the output by a fixed factor, and the local rate of change equals the current value. The exponential series gives one construction; an equivalent characterization is the unique solution of a differential equation y′=y, y(0)=1.
For a concrete example, y(t)=10e0.2t starts at 10 and satisfies y′=0.2y. The absolute derivative increases with y, while the relative rate y′/y stays 0.2. At t=5, y=10e≈27.1828 and y′≈5.43656. The exponential function therefore models accumulation proportional to what is already present, rather than addition of a fixed amount at every step. A positive constant rate gives exponential growth; a negative one gives exponential decay.
Every positive real base b=1 fits the same construction through bx=exlnb. Thus its derivative is (lnb)bx: base e is special because lne=1. The exponential function is also unchanged in form by differentiation and integration, helping explain its repeated appearance in linear ordinary differential equations. Its real definition, inverse relationship, and derivative rules are developed in OpenStax, integrals, exponential functions, and logarithms.

Fundamental theorem of calculus (dxd​∫ax​f(t)dt=f(x))

Words: 303 Articles: 1
Calculus OurBigBook.com
The fundamental theorem of calculus says that accumulation and local change undo one another, under appropriate regularity conditions. If f is a continuous function on [a,b] and
A(x)=∫ax​f(t)dt,
(65)
then A is differentiable for a<x<b and A′(x)=f(x). Conversely, if G is an antiderivative of f on this interval, continuous at its endpoints, then
∫ab​f(x)dx=G(b)−G(a).​
(66)
The first statement turns an integral into a function with a known derivative; the second turns an entire accumulation into two endpoint values.
For f(t)=1+2t, accumulation from zero gives A(x)=x+x2. At x=2, its derivative is A′(2)=5, exactly the current value f(2). The accumulated value there is A(2)=6, and by x=3 it has reached A(3)=12. The accumulated quantity and its rate are different functions, linked by differentiation.
This connection makes the theorem useful far beyond geometric area. It recovers displacement from velocity, gives a probability from a probability density function, and converts many differential equations into integral equations. The striking economy is that information spread across a whole interval can sometimes be recovered from an antiderivative at its two boundaries.
A short explanation of the first part is that
hA(x+h)−A(x)​=h1​∫xx+h​f(t)dt
(67)
is the local average of f. Continuity makes this average approach f(x). For the second part, G−A has zero derivative and is constant by the mean value theorem. These are the ideas behind the proof; the endpoint and regularity conditions make them valid.
An early geometric form of this connection appears in Isaac Barrow's Lectiones geometricae (1670), Lecture X, Proposition 11. The original volume is catalogued by CESIMA, and Michael Nauenberg's historical research reproduces and examines the geometric argument.[ref][ref]

Mean value theorem (f′(c)=b−af(b)−f(a)​)

Words: 493 Articles: 2
Calculus OurBigBook.com
The mean value theorem says that an average rate of change is attained as an instantaneous rate somewhere between the endpoints. Let a<b and let the real-valued function f:[a,b]→R be continuous on the closed interval [a,b] and differentiable on the open interval (a,b). Then there exists c∈(a,b) such that
f′(c)=b−af(b)−f(a)​.
(68)
The right-hand side is the slope of the secant line joining (a,f(a)) to (b,f(b)); the left-hand side is the slope of the tangent line at (c,f(c)). The derivative need not be continuous, and the function need not be differentiable at the endpoints. [ref]
For the polynomial f(x)=x2 on [1,3], the secant line has slope (9−1)/(3−1)=4. Since the derivative is f′(x)=2x, the required interior point is c=2. The tangent line there is y=4+4(x−2)=4x−4, whereas the secant line is y=1+4(x−1)=4x−3. Their equal slopes make them parallel, but they are distinct straight lines: the theorem equates rates, not heights.
The practical strength is that the unknown point c can disappear from an estimate. Under the same hypotheses, if the derivative satisfies ∣f′(x)∣≤M throughout (a,b), where M≥0, then
∣f(b)−f(a)∣=∣f′(c)∣∣b−a∣≤M∣b−a∣.
(69)
Applying this to every subinterval proves Lipschitz continuity with Lipschitz bound M. For example, f(x)=x2 on [1,3] has ∣f′(x)∣≤6, so an input change of size at most δ changes its output by at most 6δ, as long as both inputs lie in that interval. A local derivative bound therefore controls finite changes without computing an integral. The sign of the derivative similarly gives the derivative criterion for monotonicity.
Taking M=0 shows that a function with zero derivative throughout a real interval is a constant function, provided it is continuous at any included endpoints. The interval condition is essential: on the domain of a function (−2,−1)∪(1,2), the function equal to zero on the left interval and one on the right interval has zero derivative everywhere. It is a locally constant function, yet not a constant function on the whole domain of a function. The mean value theorem cannot cross the gap.
A concise proof subtracts the secant line: set m=(f(b)−f(a))/(b−a) and h(x)=f(x)−f(a)−m(x−a). Then h(a)=h(b)=0, and Rolle's theorem gives an interior point with h′(c)=f′(c)−m=0. The geometric idea is to remove the average trend and find a horizontal tangent line in what remains.

and the derivative does not exist at zero because the one-sided derivatives disagree. Every existing derivative in the interior is nonzero. The corner fails a hypothesis of both Rolle's theorem and the mean value theorem, so neither conclusion is guaranteed.
For a short proof, the extreme value theorem supplies a greatest and a least value on [a,b]. If f is a constant function, every interior point works. Otherwise at least one of these values differs from the common endpoint value, so it is attained at an interior extremum. At an interior local maximum or local minimum, differentiability forces the derivative to be zero: the difference quotients from the two sides have opposite weak signs and the same limit.
This turns repeated values into information about derivatives. Two distinct roots of a polynomial force a root of its derivative between them; iterating this idea gives the Rolle root count with multiplicities. More generally, a differentiable function with nonzero derivative throughout a real interval cannot repeat a value there, hence is injective. The beauty is that knowing only two equal values guarantees an exact local feature somewhere between them.

If a nonzero real polynomial has N roots in an open real interval, counted with multiplicity of a root, its derivative has at least N−1 roots in that interval, also counted with multiplicity, provided N≥1. Each root of multiplicity m becomes a root of the derivative of multiplicity m−1. The Rolle theorem supplies one further root between each pair of distinct consecutive roots. Thus k distinct roots of multiplicities mj​ give at least ∑j​(mj​−1)+(k−1)=N−1 derivative roots.

Taylor's theorem

Words: 883 Articles: 13
Calculus OurBigBook.com
Taylor's theorem expresses a sufficiently differentiable function as a finite Taylor polynomial plus a Taylor remainder. One convenient version assumes f is n+1 times continuously differentiable on the segment between a and x. Then
f(x)=Tn,a​(x)+Rn,a​(x),Rn,a​(x)=(n+1)!f(n+1)(ξ)​(x−a)n+1
(73)
for some intermediate point ξ, when x=a. Thus a bound ∣f(n+1)∣≤M on that segment gives ∣Rn,a​(x)∣≤M∣x−a∣n+1/(n+1)!. The intermediate point usually need not be computed: bounding the derivative throughout the segment is enough. This is why local approximation can yield reliable numerical bounds. A finite Taylor polynomial does not require an infinite Taylor series to represent the function.
Historically, the Royal Society holds Brook Taylor's letter of 26 July 1712 to John Machin. Its catalogue connects his work on Kepler's second law with the expansion later published in the 1715 Methodus incrementorum directa et inversa. This is a documented route from an orbital calculation to a general approximation method, rather than a claim that every earlier use of such expansions began with Taylor. See Royal Society archive, letter MS/82/2.

Intermediate value theorem

Words: 1k Articles: 9
Continuous function OurBigBook.com
The intermediate value theorem says that a real-valued continuous function cannot skip a value between two of its outputs. Let a<b and let f:[a,b]→R be a continuous function on the entire closed interval [a,b]. Then
min{f(a),f(b)}≤y≤max{f(a),f(b)}⟹there exists c∈[a,b] with f(c)=y.
(82)
The word "between" includes both endpoint values: choose c=a when y=f(a), or c=b when y=f(b). If y is strictly between them, every such c lies in the open interval (a,b). Continuity on [a,b] means continuity at every interior point, together with the endpoint one-sided limits limx→a+​f(x)=f(a) and limx→b−​f(x)=f(b). No derivative is required.[ref]
For finding a zero of a function, the useful special case is
f(a)f(b)<0⟹there exists c∈(a,b) with f(c)=0.
(83)
Strictly opposite endpoint signs certify a root bracket, because zero is strictly between f(a) and f(b). If an endpoint value is already zero, that endpoint supplies a zero of a function directly; an interior zero of a function need not exist. For example, f(x)=x on [0,1] has its only zero of a function at the left endpoint. The intermediate value theorem guarantees existence, but neither uniqueness nor a necessary sign-change test. Its numerical usefulness is that the bisection method can turn existence into successively tighter root brackets.

The polynomial function h(x)=x3−x=x(x−1)(x+1) is a continuous function on [−3/2,3/2], with h(−3/2)=−15/8 and h(3/2)=15/8. The intermediate value theorem guarantees at least one zero of a function in the interior, while the polynomial factorization displays three: −1,0,1. Thus strict opposite signs do not establish uniqueness.

has j(−1)=−1 and j(1)=1, yet no zero of a function. Its jump discontinuity at zero is exactly where the continuity hypothesis fails. A drawn vertical connector would be misleading: the function graph contains neither the intermediate heights nor a zero of a function at that jump. Even continuity only on the interior is insufficient: setting q(x)=−1 for 0≤x<1 and q(1)=1 gives opposite endpoint signs on [0,1] with no zero of a function, because the left one-sided limit at 1 is not q(1).
The polynomial function t(x)=x2 on [−1,1] is a continuous function, and t(−1)=t(1)=1, yet t(0)=0. Its root of a polynomial at zero has multiplicity of a root two. The function graph touches its horizontal tangent line there and stays positive on both sides: existence of a zero of a function does not require a sign change. For a short proof outline, endpoint values give the non-strict cases immediately. If y is strictly between f(a) and f(b), apply the bisection method to the continuous function g(x)=f(x)−y. A midpoint with g=0 finishes the proof. Otherwise retain nested intervals [ak​,bk​] with strictly opposite signs and widths (b−a)2−k. The nested interval theorem, using completeness of the real numbers, gives a common point c to which both endpoint sequences converge. After reversing the sign of g if necessary, g(ak​)<0<g(bk​). Continuity makes both endpoint value sequences converge to g(c), forcing g(c)≤0 and g(c)≥0, hence f(c)=y. The original endpoint values differ from y, so c∈(a,b). The chain rule calculates the derivative of a function composition by combining local rates. If the inner function f is differentiable at a and the outer function g is differentiable at f(a), then

The evaluation point matters: the outer derivative is evaluated at the inner output f(a), not at a. A small input change first scales by f′(a); the resulting intermediate change then scales by g′(f(a)). In terms of linear approximations, composing those two local descriptions multiplies their scale factors. [ref].
For example, h(x)=sin(x2) applies a quadratic function and then the sine. With f(x)=x2 and g(u)=sinu, the chain rule gives

Here all angles are in radians. Near x=1, increasing the input by Δx changes x2 by about 2Δx, and the sine changes by about cos1 times that intermediate change. For Δx=0.01, the linear approximation predicts an output increase of 0.0108060; the exact increase is sin(1.0201)−sin1≈0.0106894.
The same rule handles several nested stages. For h=g∘f∘k, the derivative is h′(x)=g′(f(k(x)))f′(k(x))k′(x) under the corresponding differentiability assumptions. Writing each intermediate output prevents evaluating a derivative at the wrong stage. It also makes the chain rule useful for propagating sensitivities through a mathematical model, where one measured quantity influences another through several transformations.
For a quick proof idea, replace f near a by its linear approximation, then replace g near f(a) by its linear approximation. The composite leading term is their product; differentiability ensures the remaining error is smaller than the original input change. This argument still applies when f′(a)=0, so the informal cancellation dh/dx=(dh/du)(du/dx) should not be interpreted as division by a possibly zero finite change. The hypotheses are sufficient, but are not necessary for every composite to be differentiable, as the nondifferentiable inner function with a differentiable nondegenerate composite example shows.

Monotonic function

Words: 1k Articles: 11
Calculus OurBigBook.com
A real-valued function f:D→R, with domain of a function D⊆R in the usual order of the real numbers, is a monotonic function if it is either a nondecreasing function throughout D or a nonincreasing function throughout D. The same direction must work for every pair x<y in D. Being a strictly increasing function on one part and a strictly decreasing function on another does not make the whole function monotone: for example, x2 on the real line changes direction at zero. A constant function is both a nondecreasing function and a nonincreasing function.
The word "increasing" is ambiguous across textbooks: some allow equal outputs and some require unequal outputs. Use nondecreasing function for the weak inequality and strictly increasing function for the strict inequality; use nonincreasing function and strictly decreasing function in the other direction. Neither continuity nor differentiability is part of the definition of a monotonic function.
Strict monotonicity gives injectivity, so an equation f(x)=b has at most one solution and an inverse function exists on the image of a function. Weak monotonicity permits repeated outputs and jumps. In probability theory, a cumulative distribution function is a nondecreasing function; its quantile function uses a generalized inverse to handle those flat parts and jumps. Monotonicity alone does not guarantee continuity, even for a strictly increasing function.

Hessian matrix (Hessf)

Words: 938 Articles: 6
Multivariable calculus OurBigBook.com
The Hessian matrix describes how the slope of a function changes in different directions. For a real-valued function f with continuous second partial derivatives on an open subset of Rn, it is
Hf​(x)=(∂xi​∂xj​∂2f​(x))i,j=1n​.
(118)
The symmetry of second derivatives makes Hf​ a symmetric matrix under these hypotheses. It is also the Jacobian matrix of the gradient: near x, a small displacement h changes ∇f by Hf​(x)h+o(∥h∥). Thus the gradient measures the current slope, while the Hessian measures its local variation. [ref]
For example, take the quadratic form
q(x,y)=x2+2xy+3y2.
(119)
Its gradient and Hessian matrix are
∇q=(2x+2y,2x+6y)T,Hq​=(22​26​).
(120)
The only critical point is the origin. Completing the square gives q=(x+y)2+2y2, so the origin is a strict global minimum. The eigenvalues 4−22​ and 4+22​ are both positive, recovering the same conclusion from the positive definiteness of the Hessian. Its eigenvectors identify the rotated directions in which the quadratic form has its smallest and largest bending.
For a fixed vector v, restriction to a straight line gives the directional interpretation
dt2d2​f(x+tv)​t=0​=vTHf​(x)v.
(121)
This is the quadratic form associated with the Hessian matrix. For a unit eigenvector v, it equals the corresponding eigenvalue. Opposite signs therefore mean that some directions bend upwards and others downwards. The second-derivative test turns this information into a classification when the gradient vanishes.
The same object is useful for computation. Newton's method in optimization chooses a displacement h by solving Hf​(x)h=−∇f(x) when the Hessian matrix is an invertible matrix; this makes the gradient of the local quadratic model vanish. For the displayed q, the equation gives h=−(x,y)T, so one exact step reaches the minimum from any starting point. For a general function, a Hessian with opposite-sign eigenvalues or a large condition number need not give a useful minimizing step, and the local minimum need not be a global minimum.
The name honors Otto Hesse. [ref] An older geometric use is the Hessian criterion for flexes of a plane cubic, connecting a determinant of second partial derivatives with inflection points of an algebraic curve. Hesse's 1844 paper Über die Wendepuncte der Curven dritter Ordnung is an early source on that geometric problem. [ref]

Two negative leading even powers give a strict local maximum, two positive ones a strict local minimum, and opposite signs give a saddle. Looking along the coordinate directions and bounding the separated terms avoids an inconclusive quadratic test.

For f−​, the restrictions f−​(t,0)=t4>0 and f−​(0,t)=−t4<0 for t=0 show that the origin is a saddle point of a scalar function. Second-derivative test

Words: 284 Articles: 1
Hessian matrix OurBigBook.com
Let f have continuous second partial derivatives near an interior critical point x∗​ of an open subset of Rn, with ∇f(x∗​)=0. The Hessian matrix gives the following sufficient conditions:
  • All eigenvalues positive: a strict local minimum.
  • All eigenvalues negative: a strict local maximum.
  • Both positive and negative eigenvalues: a saddle point of a scalar function.
A positive semidefinite or negative semidefinite Hessian matrix with a zero eigenvalue does not settle the classification. The higher-order test for separated extrema gives two quartic examples with exactly the same zero Hessian. These conditions apply to an interior critical point; a boundary optimum or a constrained optimization problem requires attention to the allowed directions. [ref]
The proof outline is the Taylor expansion
f(x∗​+h)−f(x∗​)=21​hTHf​(x∗​)h+o(∥h∥2).
(124)
For a positive-definite matrix, the smallest eigenvalue supplies a positive bound proportional to ∥h∥2, which dominates the remainder for small enough h. Negate the function for the local maximum case. For opposite-sign eigenvalues, choose the two corresponding eigenvectors: the leading terms have opposite signs along their lines.
There are also necessary conditions. At an interior local minimum, the Hessian matrix is positive semidefinite; at an interior local maximum, it is negative semidefinite. Restriction to each straight line reduces this to the one-variable second derivative condition. Since the Laplacian is the trace of the Hessian, it is nonnegative at such a local minimum and nonpositive at such a local maximum. The sign of the Laplacian alone is insufficient: x2−2y2 has negative Laplacian but a saddle point of a scalar function at the origin.

Equal-sign coordinates give global maxima and opposite-sign coordinates give global minima, with values ±1/(2eα). The Hessian matrix there is −4αxye−1I. Their distance from the origin is α−1/2, so as α↓0 they escape every compact region. At nonpositive α the origin is the only critical point. This illustrates why the number of critical points on an unbounded domain can change without a finite degenerate critical point appearing.

Nondegenerate critical point

Words: 61
Hessian matrix OurBigBook.com
A critical point of a real function with continuous second partial derivatives is nondegenerate when its Hessian matrix is an invertible matrix there, equivalently when none of its eigenvalues is zero. A positive-definite matrix gives a strict local minimum, a negative definite Hessian gives a strict local maximum, and opposite-sign eigenvalues give a saddle point of a scalar function. A nondegenerate critical point need not be an extremum: x2−y2 has Hessian matrix diag(2,−2), which is an invertible matrix.
Such critical points are the local building blocks of Morse theory.

Vector calculus

Words: 3k Articles: 76
Multivariable calculus OurBigBook.com
Vector calculus studies differentiation and integration of scalar fields and vector fields. Three operators answer different local questions: the gradient describes change of a scalar value, the divergence describes net outward flow, and the curl describes local circulation. Their associated integral theorems turn local derivatives into measurements along paths and across boundaries.
The difference between divergence and curl is especially visible in two smooth vector fields on three-dimensional Euclidean space:
F(x,y,z)=(x,y,0),G(x,y,z)=(−y,x,0).
(125)
At each point they have the same Euclidean norm x2+y2​, but their directions differ. For F, ∇⋅F=2 and ∇×F=0. For G, ∇⋅G=0 and ∇×G=(0,0,2). One expands radially in each horizontal plane; the other describes rigid rotation.
Around the counterclockwise unit circle in the plane z=0, F is normal to the boundary and has zero tangential component. Its outward planar flux integral is 2π, while its line integral around the circle is zero. For G the values are reversed: outward planar flux is zero, and circulation is 2π. The divergence and curl predict exactly which boundary measurement survives.
Why is this useful? A velocity field can move material through a boundary or circulate it within a region. Conservation of mass connects its divergence with density changes through the continuity equation; its curl is vorticity. In electromagnetism, the Maxwell equations use the same operators to connect electric fields, magnetic fields, and their sources. The common mathematical language lets the same integral calculations work across different physical models. [ref].
The geometric framework behind these operators is developed in differential forms. The Generalized Stokes theorem unifies the fundamental theorem for line integrals, Green theorem, Stokes theorem, and divergence theorem. In coordinates their formulas look different, but each relates accumulation over a region to a measurement on its boundary.
Wilson's Vector Analysis, published in 1901, was based on J. Willard Gibbs's lectures at Yale. Wilson's preface explains that examples from geometry, mechanics, and physics are interspersed with the mathematical development, so readers encounter applications as soon as they have the tools to understand them. That is a useful way to approach vector calculus: learn each operation through a measurement it makes possible. [ref].

Conservative vector field

Words: 303 Articles: 4
Vector calculus OurBigBook.com
A vector field X is conservative when X=∇Φ for a potential of a conservative vector field Φ. On a simply connected open subset of R3, every continuously differentiable curl-free vector field is conservative. Locally this follows from the Poincaré lemma applied to the differential one-form Xi​dxi; globally, simple connectivity makes its line integral independent of the path. The fundamental theorem for line integrals expresses that path independence as the difference of the potential at the endpoints.

Periods obstruct a periodic potential
Words: 70
Conservative vector field OurBigBook.com
If a periodic vector field has a periodic potential of a conservative vector field, the line integral between points separated by a period vector must vanish, since it is the potential difference. A periodic gradient field need not satisfy this: the constant field (1,2) on the plane has potential x+2y, but its integrals over the two unit translations are 1 and 2. On the periodic quotient these translation integrals are nonzero periods, obstructing a single-valued potential there.
Potential of a conservative vector field (X=∇Φ)
Words: 126 Articles: 1
Conservative vector field OurBigBook.com
A potential for a conservative vector field X is a function with scalar values Φ whose gradient is X. Potentials differ by a constant on each connected component. The fundamental theorem for line integrals gives ∫γ​X⋅dx=Φ(γ(1))−Φ(γ(0)). In mechanics a conservative force is conventionally written −∇V, so its potential energy is V=−Φ. This spatial potential differs from the scalar potential V(ϕ) that denotes the derivative-free energy density of a scalar field.

Divergence theorem

Words: 419 Articles: 5
Vector calculus OurBigBook.com
Let V be a bounded region in Euclidean space with piecewise smooth boundary and outward unit normal vector n. For a continuously differentiable vector field F on a neighborhood of its closure,
∫V​∇⋅FdV=∫∂V​F⋅ndS.
(147)
The total outward flux equals the accumulated divergence inside. Contributions across shared internal faces cancel when a region is divided into small pieces.
For F=(x,y,z) on a ball of radius R, the divergence is 3, giving 3(4πR3/3)=4πR3. On the boundary, F⋅n=R, so the surface integral is also R(4πR2)=4πR3​. This agreement turns the derivative into a geometric flux measurement. The required regularity matters: a singular field at the center cannot be included without checking its contribution separately.

The theorem applies to piecewise smooth boundaries, with singular points removed by a limiting argument when necessary.

This is the scalar-gradient analogue of the usual flux identity.

On an oriented Riemannian manifold with boundary, the divergence of a Riemannian vector field obeys the displayed integral identity for smooth compactly supported vector fields X, or for arbitrary smooth X if the manifold is compact. Here N is the outward unit normal vector and the boundary has the outward-normal-first boundary orientation. Its induced Riemannian volume form is j∗ιN​ωg​. Splitting X into its normal and tangential components gives j∗ιX​ωg​=g(X,N)ωg​​, since a top form vanishes on n boundary-tangent arguments. Apply the Stokes theorem to dιX​ωg​=(divX)ωg​.
Without a support or decay condition, flux at infinity can invalidate the result even if the integrals converge. On [0,∞) with Riemannian metric dx2, X=(arctanx)∂x​ has boundary flux zero but integral of divergence π/2.

Stokes theorem

Words: 217 Articles: 2
Vector calculus OurBigBook.com
Let S be an oriented smooth surface with piecewise smooth boundary, and let F be a continuously differentiable vector field on a neighborhood of S. With the compatible boundary direction determined by the right-hand rule,
∫S​(∇×F)⋅ndS=∮∂S​F⋅dx.
(149)
For G=(−y,x,0) on the horizontal unit disc with upward normal, the left side is 2 times its area, giving 2π. The counterclockwise boundary has tangential field of magnitude one and circumference 2π, giving the same line integral. Reversing the surface normal reverses the boundary direction and both signs. The theorem replaces a circulation calculation with a surface integral of the curl, whichever is easier.

Change of variables formula (∫T(S)​f(x)dx=∫S​f(T(u))∣detDT(u)∣du)

Words: 1k Articles: 22
Multivariable calculus OurBigBook.com
The change of variables formula expresses an integral in coordinates that make its integrand or its region simpler. Three ingredients change together: the region, the function being integrated, and the element of area or volume. The last change is measured by the absolute Jacobian determinant; forgetting it amounts to counting transformed cells as though their sizes had stayed the same.
In one dimension, substitution is the integrated chain rule. If g is continuously differentiable on [a,b] and f is continuous on its image, then
∫ab​f(g(x))g′(x)dx=∫g(a)g(b)​f(u)du.
(150)
These are directed definite integrals: if g decreases, the transformed endpoints reverse. This identity does not require g to be injective, because an antiderivative composed with g already accounts for any backtracking.[ref]
For a concrete computation, set u=1+x2, so du=2xdx. The endpoints x=0,1 become u=1,2:
∫01​1+x22x​dx=∫12​udu​=[lnu]12​=ln2≈0.693147.
(151)
The numerator is precisely the derivative of the expression in the denominator. Substitution reveals the familiar natural logarithm hidden inside this rational function. Keeping the original endpoints after changing the integrand would describe a different integral.
For the elementary two-dimensional theorem, let T:U→V be a C1 diffeomorphism between open sets in the plane, let S⊂U be a bounded region with piecewise smooth boundary, and let f be continuous on T(S), with the displayed integrals finite. Then
∬T(S)​f(x,y)dxdy=∬S​f(T(u,v))∣detDT(u,v)∣dudv.
(152)
Here DT is the Jacobian matrix. The diffeomorphism assumption means a bijection with a continuously differentiable inverse, and ensures a nonzero Jacobian determinant. This excludes overlapping sheets; the more general area formula handles multiplicity.[ref]
Take S=[0,1]2 and the linear map
T(u,v)=(2u+v,v),DT=(20​11​),detDT=2.
(153)
Its inverse is (u,v)=((x−y)/2,y). The square becomes a parallelogram with vertices (0,0),(2,0),(3,1),(1,1): base two, height one, area two. Consequently ∬T(S)​1dxdy=∬S​2dudv=2. A nonconstant integrand changes too: ∬T(S)​xdxdy=∫01​∫01​(2u+v)2dudv=3.
The direction of the map matters when selecting the factor. Here T goes from the new coordinates to the original coordinates, so the factor is two. Its inverse has Jacobian determinant 1/2, appropriate for converting area in the opposite direction. Writing down the map before computing its Jacobian matrix prevents a reciprocal-factor error.
Now reflect the image vertically: T(u,v)=(2u+v,−v) has Jacobian determinant −2, but still produces area two. The sign records reversal of the orientation of a vector space; ordinary area uses its absolute value. For oriented differential forms, the pullback of a differential form instead retains the signed determinant.[ref]
The geometric beauty is that a nonlinear differentiable map has a local linear approximation: tiny rectangles behave approximately like these parallelograms. Summing their scaled contributions gives the change of variables formula. In polar coordinates this factor is r, explaining dxdy=rdrdθ; equal angular steps cover more area farther from the origin. Choosing suitable coordinates can simplify both the boundary and the integrand.[ref]

Inverse function theorem

Words: 2k Articles: 10
Differentiable map OurBigBook.com
The inverse function theorem answers a practical question: can nearby outputs be used to recover nearby inputs uniquely and smoothly? Its useful surprise is that a nonlinear function can be tested using its linear derivative. If the first-order changes preserve all input directions, then, on a sufficiently small region, the nonlinear map can also be reversed. This is the basis for treating a nonlinear map as a coordinate transformation.
Precisely, let f:U→Rn be continuously differentiable on an open subset U of Euclidean space, let a∈U, and put b=f(a). If Df(a) is an invertible linear map, there are open neighbourhoods U0​ of a and V0​ of b such that f:U0​→V0​ is a bijection with a continuously differentiable inverse function g. Thus this restriction is a diffeomorphism. In coordinates the test is detDf(a)=0, using the Jacobian determinant. The derivative of a local inverse map is obtained by inverting the Jacobian matrix, at the corresponding input. [ref]
For a one-dimensional example, f(x)=x2 has f′(1)=2. Near x=1, the inverse function is g(y)=y​, and the inverse function rule gives g′(1)=1/2. But x2 has no inverse function on the whole real line, since x and −x give the same output. The theorem supplies a local restriction, not global injectivity. At zero, the derivative test fails; the nonnegative branch still has a square root inverse, but that inverse has no finite derivative at zero. [ref]
Here is a two-dimensional example with an invertible derivative everywhere and infinitely repeated outputs:
f(s,θ)=(escosθ,essinθ),Df(s,θ)=es(cosθsinθ​−sinθcosθ​),detDf=e2s>0.
(161)
The exponential function turns s into a positive radius, while θ is the angle in polar coordinates. Restricting, for example, to ∣s∣<0.35 and ∣θ∣<0.6 produces the reversible patch pictured below. On its image, with Cartesian coordinates (u,v) and u>0, the inverse function is
s=21​log(u2+v2),θ=arctan(v/u).
(162)
The arctangent selects the angle near zero. Without an angle restriction, f(s,θ+2πk)=f(s,θ) for every integer k, so there is no single global inverse function. This map is a local diffeomorphism but is not injective.
The short proof idea is to correct a guessed input using the inverse linear response. With A=Df(a), solving f(x)=y is equivalent to finding a fixed point of
Ty​(x)=x+A−1(y−f(x)).
(163)
At a, the derivative DTy​(a)=I−A−1Df(a) vanishes. Continuity makes Ty​ a contraction mapping on a sufficiently small closed ball, which it maps into itself when y is sufficiently close to b. The contraction mapping theorem then gives existence and uniqueness there. Establishing the smooth dependence on y completes the inverse theorem. This explains why the nonlinearity can be tolerated: its correction has a small local slope.[ref]
Derivative of a local inverse map (Dg(y)=[Df(g(y))]−1)
Words: 95
Inverse function theorem OurBigBook.com
For the continuously differentiable inverse function g supplied by the inverse function theorem, the chain rule applied to f(g(y))=y gives
Df(g(y))Dg(y)=I,Dg(y)=[Df(g(y))]−1.
(164)
Here I is the identity matrix. The matrix inverse is taken at the recovered input g(y), not at the output y. In one dimension this is the inverse function rule g′(y)=1/f′(g(y)).
The formula also describes sensitivity. For a small output perturbation h, differentiability gives g(y+h)−g(y)=Dg(y)h+o(∥h∥). A large operator norm of Dg(y) permits large amplification in some directions. In the square root example, g′(y)=1/(2y​) grows without bound as positive y approaches zero. Existence of a local inverse function therefore does not imply that recovery is insensitive to measurement error.
Constant rank theorem
Words: 317 Articles: 1
Inverse function theorem OurBigBook.com
The constant rank theorem separates the directions a smooth map preserves from the directions it forgets. If a smooth map from an open subset of Rm to Rn has derivative of constant rank r on a neighbourhood of a point, there are local coordinate transformations in source and target in which it becomes
(x1,…,xm)⟼(x1,…,xr,0,…,0).
(165)
It keeps r coordinates, discards the other m−r, and inserts n−r zeros. This is stronger than simplifying the Jacobian matrix at one point: it straightens the actual nonlinear map on a neighbourhood. [ref]
For a worked example, take
f(x,y)=(x+y,(x+y)2),Df(x,y)=(12(x+y)​12(x+y)​).
(166)
The two columns agree, and the first row is nonzero, so the rank is exactly one everywhere. The image of a function is the parabola b=a2. Every line x+y=a is a fiber mapping to the same point (a,a2).
Choose input coordinates u=x+y, v=x−y, and output coordinates α=a, β=b−a2. Both coordinate transformations are diffeomorphisms: their inverses are x=(u+v)/2, y=(u−v)/2 and a=α, b=β+α2. In these coordinates,
(u,v)⟼(u,u2)⟼(u,0).
(167)
The curved image has become a straight line, and the unused coordinate v is explicit.
Constant rank on a neighbourhood is essential. The map (x,y)↦(x,y2) has rank one when y=0 and two when y=0, so the constant rank theorem does not supply one rank-one form across that line. By contrast, the full-rank square case of the theorem forgets no coordinates and recovers the inverse function theorem. The usefulness is that curved fibers and images can often be studied through this simpler local form.
Rank-one level curves from a characteristic differential equation (y′=−fx​/fy​)
Words: 62
Constant rank theorem OurBigBook.com
For a smooth map F=(f,g) on the plane with zero Jacobian determinant and fy​=0, set e=gy​/fy​. The determinant identity gives ∇g=e∇f. Along a curve solving y′=−fx​/fy​, both f and g have zero derivative. Local existence and uniqueness for this smooth differential equation through every nearby point produce a local foliation by curves of constant F.
Local diffeomorphism
Words: 283 Articles: 2
Inverse function theorem OurBigBook.com
A local diffeomorphism is a differentiable map that restricts near every point to a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of its target. The local inverse functions need not combine into a single global inverse function: different parts of the domain of a function can map onto the same output region.
For continuously differentiable maps between open subsets of Rn, being a local diffeomorphism is equivalent to having an invertible derivative at every point. The inverse function theorem proves one direction. For the other, the chain rule for each local inverse function gives two inverse linear maps. The periodic angle example under the inverse function theorem has this property everywhere, even though it has infinitely many inputs for every point of the punctured plane. The noninjective map with constant Jacobian determinant gives another useful distinction: even a constant nonzero Jacobian determinant need not give global injectivity.
Every local diffeomorphism is an open map. To see this, take an open subset of the source and intersect it with the neighbourhoods where the map is a diffeomorphism. Each local image is open, and their union is the full image. Thus nearby outputs remain available locally, despite the possible global ambiguity.
Noninjective map with constant Jacobian determinant (a(s,r)=es(cos(re−2s),sin(re−2s)))
Words: 61
Local diffeomorphism OurBigBook.com
The displayed smooth map from R2 to the punctured plane has Jacobian determinant one: in polar coordinates its radius is es and its angle is re−2s, so the determinant is e2se−2s=1. Nevertheless a(0,2πk)=(1,0) for every integer k. Thus a local volume-preserving map need not be injective or have bounded weighted inverse multiplicity. Compactly supported data distributed over many inverse branches disprove a determinant-only dispersion with a nonlinear velocity map estimate.
Open map
Words: 67
Local diffeomorphism OurBigBook.com
An open map sends every open subset of its source to an open subset of its target. This is an image property; continuity instead concerns preimages of open sets. A local diffeomorphism has both properties, but openness alone does not promise unique recovery of an input. In the periodic coordinate map under the inverse function theorem, open patches give open output regions while multiple angle values still give the same output.
Together, open and closed maps describe the two image-set preservation properties.
Implicit function theorem
Words: 509 Articles: 3
Inverse function theorem OurBigBook.com
An equation can define a function without giving an explicit formula for it. The implicit function theorem tells us when the constraint F(x,y)=0 determines y uniquely from nearby x, and makes the resulting function continuously differentiable. It is useful when solving an equation explicitly is cumbersome or impossible: the partial derivatives already reveal whether local recovery is possible.
Let F be a continuously differentiable map from an open subset of Rm×Rn to Rn. Suppose F(x0​,y0​)=0 and the partial derivative Dy​F(x0​,y0​) is an invertible linear map. There are open neighbourhoods U of x0​ and V of y0​ and a unique continuously differentiable function g:U→V such that, for (x,y)∈U×V,
F(x,y)=0⟺y=g(x),g(x0​)=y0​.
(168)
Thus the nearby level set is a graph of a function. The derivative of this graph is
Dg(x)=−[Dy​F(x,g(x))]−1Dx​F(x,g(x)).
(169)
The matrix inverse acts on the left; the order matters in several dimensions.
For example, take the unit circle, written as the level set F(x,y)=x2+y2−1=0. At (x0​,y0​)=(3/5,4/5), Fy​=2y0​=8/5=0, so the local upper branch is y=g(x)=1−x2​. Implicit differentiation gives
g′(x)=−Fy​Fx​​=−yx​,g′(3/5)=−3/4.​
(170)
This tangent line slope is available directly from the constraint. The negative square root branch is elsewhere on the same circle; it does not destroy uniqueness near the selected upper point.
At (1,0), however, Fy​=0 and the circle cannot be represented locally as one function y=g(x): just to the left of x=1 there are two nearby values of y. The circle is still smooth there. Since Fx​=2=0, use the other coordinate instead: x=h(y)=1−y2​, with h′(0)=0. A failed coordinate choice is different from a geometric singularity.
The derivative condition is sufficient, not necessary for every possible implicit graph. For F(x,y)=y3, the entire zero set is the smooth graph y=0, even though Fy​ vanishes there. In this case the defining equation itself has a degenerate derivative; the theorem's test gives no conclusion.
The connection to the inverse function theorem is particularly elegant. Augment the constraint to the map H(x,y)=(x,F(x,y)), whose Jacobian matrix is
DH=(IDx​F​0Dy​F​).
(171)
Its determinant is detDy​F. When this is nonzero, locally invert H and set its second output to zero. The recovered second input is g(x). In this way an implicit constraint becomes an ordinary inverse function problem. [ref]

Implicit differentiation
Words: 98 Articles: 1
Implicit function theorem OurBigBook.com
Implicit differentiation differentiates an identity F(x,y(x))=0 along a differentiable branch and uses the chain rule to solve for its derivative:
Fx​+Fy​y′=0,y′=−Fy​Fx​​(Fy​=0).
(172)
The partial derivatives Fx​,Fy​ treat x,y as independent coordinates before evaluating on the branch. The implicit function theorem justifies the branch's local existence and regularity under its hypotheses; differentiating alone does not establish either. For the unit circle at (3/5,4/5), this calculation yields the tangent line y−4/5=−(3/4)(x−3/5).

Integration by parts (∫udv=uv−∫vdu)

Words: 315 Articles: 1
Calculus OurBigBook.com
Integration by parts transfers a derivative from one factor of a product to the other, while keeping an endpoint contribution. Its usefulness comes from choosing which factor becomes simpler when differentiated, and which has an accessible antiderivative. The integral is then replaced by a boundary term minus another integral.
For real continuously differentiable functions u,v on [a,b], the precise definite integral formula is
∫ab​u(x)v′(x)dx=[u(x)v(x)]ab​−∫ab​u′(x)v(x)dx,[uv]ab​=u(b)v(b)−u(a)v(a).
(173)
In the shorter notation, du=u′(x)dx and dv=v′(x)dx, giving ∫udv=uv−∫vdu for indefinite integrals, with a constant of integration understood. The product rule says (uv)′=u′v+uv′; the fundamental theorem of calculus turns its integral into the endpoint difference. Thus the formula packages a differentiation rule into a tool for integration.[ref]
For example, choose u=x and dv=exdx. Then du=dx and v=ex, since the exponential function is its own derivative:
∫01​xexdx=[xex]01​−∫01​exdx=e−(e−1)=1.
(174)
The boundary term is e≈2.718282; the remaining integral is e−1≈1.718282. Their difference is exactly one. The endpoint product alone would overcount, because its derivative includes u′v=ex as well as the desired uv′=xex.
In the figure, the area under (xex)′=(1+x)ex is the endpoint contribution e. Its lower band has area e−1, and its upper band has thickness xex and area one. This decomposition makes the subtraction visible. The endpoint contribution is a difference of product values; it need not equal the area under either factor separately.
The same choice repeatedly lowers the degree of a polynomial when integrating a polynomial times an exponential function, while choosing u=lnx gives ∫lnxdx=xlnx−x+C for x>0. More broadly, moving a derivative onto a convenient test function is the mechanism behind a weak derivative. Always evaluate the boundary term: it disappears only when the relevant endpoint values justify doing so, often through a boundary condition.

Odd function OurBigBook.com
An odd extension of a function f on the positive half-line is f​(r)=f(r) for r>0 and f​(r)=−f(−r) for r<0. At zero it is set to zero when the boundary value is zero.
